title: Feminist Perspectives on Sex and Gender

summaries.example: Imagine a school where girls are told they should only play quietly and boys are told they should never cry. Those messages are not facts about what children can do. They are social expectations. A child may learn them from family, friends, toys, books, or television, but learned expectations can also change.
summaries.summary: This entry explains debates in feminist philosophy about sex and gender. Some feminists use sex for bodily features and gender for social meanings, roles, and expectations. This distinction was meant to challenge biological determinism—the idea that biology decides how women and men must think or act. Feminist philosophers have suggested that gender can be learned through socialization, shaped by unequal power, or expressed through repeated actions. Other philosophers question whether sex and gender can be separated so neatly. They point out that bodies are understood through social ideas and that people’s experiences differ across cultures, races, classes, and identities. The entry also asks how feminism can speak about women as a group without pretending that all women share one experience. It discusses views that connect women through shared social conditions, family resemblances, social positions, or political struggles. The overall debate remains open: philosophers disagree about the best, most useful, or correct account of gender.
key_ideas: Some feminists separate sex, which concerns bodily features, from gender, which concerns social roles and expectations.
Feminists have challenged the idea that biology decides people’s personalities, abilities, or place in society.
People can learn gender expectations from families, schools, toys, stories, and other parts of culture.
There is no single agreement about exactly what gender means or how the words woman and man should be used.
Some philosophers argue that ideas about gender should include differences among people, including differences in culture, race, class, and identity.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ideas about sex and gender can affect people’s choices, opportunities, treatment, and sense of belonging. Studying these ideas helps us notice when a social rule is being mistaken for a natural fact. It also encourages care: a definition that fits some people may leave out others. Thinking carefully about gender can support fairer conversations without assuming that everyone has the same life.

important_terms.definition: A movement and set of ideas aimed at ending the unfair treatment and oppression of women.
Physical features often used to classify people as female or male, such as body parts, hormones, and chromosomes.
Social ideas and expectations about being a woman, man, or another gender.
The belief that biology fixes how people must behave or what they can do.
The idea that social practices and expectations help create gender roles and traits.

questions_to_think_about: Where might children learn ideas about what girls or boys are supposed to do?
Can a person enjoy an activity even if other people call it a boy’s or girl’s activity?
Why might it be difficult to find one definition that fits every woman or every man?
How could stories, toys, or school rules give people different messages about gender?

summaries.example: Consider an athletic organization deciding who may compete in a women’s event. One policy might treat chromosomes as decisive; another might consider several bodily traits; another might focus on legal or social classification. The disagreement is not merely about one test. It reflects deeper questions about whether sex is a purely biological category, whether its boundaries are sharp, and how social institutions confer statuses. It also shows why a definition can have practical effects on people’s recognition and opportunities.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys feminist debates about what sex and gender are and how they relate. A historically influential position distinguishes sex, understood through bodily features, from gender, understood through social roles, behavior, identity, and position. This distinction challenged biological determinism, which treats biology as destiny, and opened space for explaining gender through socialization, cultural norms, and power. Yet the distinction is contested. Some accounts risk treating women as a uniform group and overlooking how race, class, culture, and other social locations shape gendered experience. Other accounts question whether sex itself is simply biological, noting that social conditions can affect bodies and that institutions and scientific practices help determine how sex is classified. Judith Butler’s influential approach argues that gender is performative: it is constituted through repeated, socially regulated acts, rather than expressing a stable inner gender core. Other philosophers defend ways of grouping women without relying on one shared essence, such as a social series or resemblance relation. Still others define gender through subordination, social position, or its role in organizing a person’s social life. These proposals raise questions about political usefulness, exclusion, self-identification, and whether gender should be abolished or transformed. Recent work also addresses genderqueer and non-binary identities as challenges to systems that treat man and woman as the only possible genders. The entry concludes that there is no settled definition of gender, although many contemporary feminist philosophers continue to treat social factors as central.
key_ideas: The sex/gender distinction was developed partly to reject biological determinism and to explain how social expectations can produce apparent differences between women and men.
Feminist theories disagree about whether gender is learned, rooted in power relations, connected to sexuality, constituted by repeated acts, or best understood through social position.
Critics of gender realism argue that accounts treating women as one uniform group can ignore differences involving race, class, culture, nationality, and sexuality.
Debates about sex also concern how bodies are classified and whether social practices influence both bodily development and the concepts used to describe bodies.
Some philosophers defend a distinction between sex and gender, while others argue that the distinction is unclear, politically unhelpful, or based on an overly simple nature-culture opposition.
A central political problem is how feminism can act in the name of women while keeping its category inclusive and avoiding a single norm of womanhood.
summaries.why_it_matters: Theories of sex and gender are not only abstract descriptions. They influence how institutions classify people, how social roles are justified, and who is recognized by feminist politics. Examining competing theories can reveal hidden assumptions—for example, that biology determines ability, that all women share one experience, or that gender categories are naturally fixed. The debate also shows why inclusive political action requires both general concepts and attention to differences among people.

important_terms.definition: A distinction some feminist theorists draw between biological features associated with female and male bodies and social meanings, roles, identities, or positions.
The view that biological features determine psychological traits, behavior, or proper social roles.
A process through which people acquire gendered expectations, behaviors, and traits through social interaction and cultural learning.
The view that genders or gendered traits are produced, at least partly, by social practices, institutions, and meanings.
A theory that members of a category share some defining feature, condition, or experience.
A view that a category can be unified without one feature shared by every member, for example through resemblance or shared social organization.
The idea that gender is produced through repeated, socially meaningful acts rather than expressing a fixed inner essence.
A classification that includes more than the exclusive alternatives of man and woman.

questions_to_think_about: What advantages does separating sex from gender provide, and what problems might the separation create?
Can a political movement represent a group whose members have no single shared experience?
How might a definition of womanhood unintentionally exclude people it was meant to include?
Are classifications such as sex merely descriptive, or can they also carry social expectations and consequences?
What would a theory of gender need to explain about non-binary identities?

summaries.example: Suppose a class chooses activities for a school fair. Some students say girls should decorate while boys should build because girls are naturally careful and boys are naturally good with tools. A feminist philosopher might ask whether these differences come from biology or from years of encouragement, practice, toys, and expectations. Another philosopher might ask whether the labels “girl” and “boy” themselves carry rules about how students should act. The class could discover that the expectations shaped who had practice, not what students were capable of doing.
summaries.summary: This entry introduces a major debate in feminist philosophy: whether sex and gender are different, and what each term means. Many feminists have used sex for biological features and gender for social roles, expectations, behavior, and identity. The point was to challenge biological determinism, the claim that biology fixes how women and men must behave. On this approach, gender differences can be socially constructed: they may be taught by families and peers, reinforced by media and institutions, or created through unequal power relations. Some theories emphasize gender socialization, while others focus on personality, sexuality, or the repeated actions through which gender appears stable. The distinction itself has critics. They argue that it may treat all women as if they have one experience, ignore differences shaped by race and class, or repeat an unfair opposition between body and mind. Some also argue that sex is not classified by biology alone: social practices can affect bodies, and institutions help decide which traits count as important. The entry then asks how feminism can refer to women as a group. Proposed answers include viewing women as a social series, as people who resemble varied examples, or as occupants of social positions shaped by inequality. Other theories treat gender as essential to social identity or connect it to reproductive possibilities and lived experience. Recent discussion expands beyond the binary, examining genderqueer and non-binary identities. The source presents these as ongoing disagreements rather than a settled dispute.
key_ideas: The sex/gender distinction was used by many feminists to oppose claims that women’s and men’s social behavior follows directly from biology.
Different theories explain gender in different ways: as learned behavior, personality, sexuality and power, repeated performance, or a social position.
A theory that treats women as one unified group may overlook how race, class, culture, nationality, and sexuality change people’s experiences.
Some philosophers argue that sex classifications are influenced by social meanings and institutions as well as by bodily traits.
Critics disagree about whether separating sex and gender is clarifying, misleading, or politically useful.
Feminist philosophy must consider how to discuss women as a group while remaining inclusive and avoiding a single model of what a woman is.
summaries.why_it_matters: The words sex and gender are used in schools, laws, medicine, sports, families, and everyday conversation. The meanings given to these words can affect who receives recognition, opportunity, or protection. Learning the philosophical debate helps students separate evidence about bodies from assumptions about behavior and notice how categories can both organize social action and leave people out. It also shows why respectful disagreement requires examining definitions and their consequences.

important_terms.definition: The idea that sex refers mainly to bodily features while gender refers mainly to social meanings, roles, behavior, or identity.
The belief that biology determines people’s behavior, abilities, or social roles.
The way families, peers, media, schools, and other social influences teach people gendered expectations.
The idea that social practices help produce gender categories or gendered traits, rather than merely describing them.
The view that all members of a group share a feature or condition that makes them members of that group.
An approach that groups people without requiring one feature shared by every member, perhaps through resemblance or shared social conditions.
The claim that gender is made real through repeated, socially understood actions and habits.
A way of understanding gender that does not assume everyone must be either a man or a woman.

questions_to_think_about: When does a social expectation become powerful enough to shape people’s opportunities or self-understanding?
Why might a definition that seems to unite a group also exclude some members?
How can two people be affected differently by the same gender rule because of race, class, or culture?
Does the fact that a category is socially constructed make it unreal, changeable, or both?
Why do non-binary identities challenge a simple two-category account of gender?
